LanceDB · LeRobot

27.6 Million Frames

Training a robot policy on DROID usually starts with a 369 GB download. We skipped the download. We trained straight from S3, with every batch drawn at random from all 27.6 million frames, and the GPUs stayed fed the whole way. Then we searched, curated and watched the same table without ever making a copy of it. And on a dataset we made messy on purpose, three queries on that table won back 14 of the 23 points of success the mess had cost.

1.7%of each step the GPUs spent waiting for data, reading from S3
37.4%for the same job with the standard pipeline reading from local disk
−33 minsaved on a 10,000-step run: 1 h 27 m instead of 2 h 00 m
+14 ptsclosed-loop success won back by three table queries, after 30% bad episodes cost 23

All measurements are from one machine with 8 H100 GPUs, reading from an S3 bucket in the same region. DROID has 27,630,375 frames in 95,658 episodes. The LIBERO result is 400 simulator rollouts per model on 4 H100s. The results that went against us are in here too.

00What we did

Here is the whole setup in one sentence, because everything below follows from it: we converted DROID to Lance, uploaded it to an S3 bucket, and pointed the trainer at the s3:// path. We never downloaded it. The trainer read 27,630,375 frames, 95,658 episodes and 369 GB of video over the network for the entire run.

Four things followed. Each one is measured later in this post.

  • The GPUs stayed busy. 10,000 steps of SmolVLA on 8 H100s took 1 h 27 m, and the GPUs waited for data only 1.7% of each step. The standard LeRobot pipeline, reading the same data from a local NVMe drive after a 384 GB download, took 2 h 00 m and waited 37.4% of the time. Both runs used the same seed and saw the same samples, so the loss curves match to four decimal places.
  • Every batch was a true random sample from all 27.6M frames. Not a window over the data, and not a shuffle buffer. Lance can read any frame from anywhere in the dataset, directly from object storage, in 36 GB of RAM. The usual shortcut is a shuffle buffer, and we measured what that shortcut costs in model quality.
  • The same table did the other work too. Embeddings, a motion-roughness score, a vector index and a full-text index all live as columns and indexes on the table the DataLoader reads. Curation queries and training use one source of truth, pinned to one version.
  • And it produced a working model. That is the part worth showing first, so here it is.

Below is an episode that neither checkpoint ever trained on. It is played in Foxglove through LeRobot's dataset viewer, which streams straight from the Lance table in S3, so nothing was downloaded to watch it. Each panel shows one action dimension three ways: what the human teleoperator did, what the policy predicted early in training, and what it predicted after 10,000 steps. Watch the gripper panel. The early checkpoint swings across the whole range, while the trained one follows the human closely:

Across 48 held-out episodes, all 48 improved. Next-action mean absolute error (MAE) dropped from 0.3259 to 0.1004. The improvement holds no matter how much the arm moves in an episode. The episode above is in the 98th percentile for motion, so it is a harder case than average.

The rest of this post is the evidence, in the order we did the work. Throughput first, then the claim that the training table can also be the index, then what the models did and how we checked them. Results that went against us are included.

01The GPUs stay busy, even from object storage

We trained SmolVLA on DROID with 8 GPUs and num_workers=4, which is LeRobot’s default. The number we track is data wait: the share of each training step the GPUs spend waiting for the data loader. This is a better measure than GPU utilisation from nvidia-smi, which barely changes when the loader stalls.

Lance kept data wait at 1.7% while doing a true global shuffle over all 27.6M frames from object storage. The standard pipeline sat at 37.4% while reading the same data from local disk. The difference is in how each reader fetches data. The upstream reader fetches one frame per call (dataset_reader.py:88), so it seeks once per frame. Lance plans the whole batch at once: one table read, one blob fetch, and the video decoders are reused.

What that means on the clock

Those were per-step rates. Here is the same 10,000-step job run to completion twice. Everything is identical except --dataset.root: same seed, same batch size, same number of workers, and a cold page cache both times.

10,000 steps, SmolVLA, 8×H100Lance · S3 upstream · local NVMe
wall clock1 h 27 m 29 s 2 h 00 m 22 s
difference— +33 min  (1.38×)
steady rate495 samples/s361 samples/s
step time0.519 s0.708 s
… of which waiting on data 1.7% 37.4%
GPU power297 W256 W
final loss0.23800.2380

No episode filter on either side. Cold page cache. Seed 100 for both runs.

The loss curves are identical to four decimal places at every logged step. Same seed, same samples, same order. It is one job served two ways, which is what makes the wall-clock comparison fair. The compute per step is the same, so the entire 33-minute gap is GPUs waiting on the loader. The lower power draw on the upstream side is that same idle time, measured a second way.

Keep the handicap in mind before quoting the ratio. Upstream read from local NVMe after a 384 GB download. Lance streamed from S3 with nothing downloaded, and did a global shuffle across all 27.6M frames. The comparison is tilted in upstream’s favour, and it still lost half an hour.

Upstream’s own no-download path never gets started. Its IterableDataset routes accelerate through a code path that concatenates every field in the batch, and every LeRobot dataset puts the task string in the batch. The result is TypeError: Can only concatenate tensors but got <class 'str'>. We reproduced this on DROID with SmolVLA on 8 GPUs, and on pusht with ACT on 2 GPUs. Lance trained without modification in every configuration.

What a shuffle buffer costs

The usual way to approximate a random shuffle without random access is a buffer. You hold N frames in RAM and sample from those. On DROID that costs 117 GB of memory with a 15,000-frame buffer and 230 GB with 40,000 frames. Lance reading random frames from S3 with no buffer at all uses 36 GB. These numbers are per process, so an 8-GPU job pays them eight times. The buffer also takes 196 seconds to produce a first batch, compared to 13 seconds for Lance.

It also costs training steps. We held the reader, the data and the step count fixed and changed only how wide the sampler’s window is. The 1,000-frame buffer that streaming uses by default was 67% worse on held-out loss at 2,500 steps and 16% worse at 10,000 steps. The gap closes over time, so it is not a hard ceiling on quality. But the windowed run at 10,000 steps still had not caught up with the shuffled run at 2,500 steps. That is about four times the steps for the same loss. Episodes average about 285 frames, so a 1,000-frame window draws every batch from three or four episodes, and the gradients within a batch are correlated. You also do not get to pick the window width. Streaming picks a random shard to start from and then samples from the buffer, and seven of the eight datasets we tried report num_shards=1. In those cases the buffer is the only randomness there is.

Two seeds. 200 episodes were sampled uniformly across the dataset and held out of training. All runs are fine-tuning. This applies to the streaming path only. The map-style reader already shuffles globally, but streaming is the only option that does not download the dataset first.

Samples per second. same job means both sides do a map-style global shuffle, but Lance reads from S3 and upstream reads from local disk after a full download, so the comparison is handicapped against us. vs streaming means both sides read remotely and neither downloads. Seven of eight datasets report num_shards=1, so streaming runs single-worker no matter how many workers you ask for.

The same-job speedup tracks how much video each sample carries. One camera gives 1.17 to 1.44×, three cameras give 2.8 to 3.1×, and DROID gives 6.5×. Three of the eight datasets cannot be shuffled at all. toto, berkeley_rpt and berkeley_autolab_ur5 raise IndexError under random access, and they do so identically on both readers. That is a frame-count defect in the source data, in more than a third of the datasets we tried.

DROID has a milder version of the same defect. It is worth being precise here, because it is easy to overclaim. Of three shuffled 10,000-step upstream runs, one died after 267 seconds with Invalid frame index=98513 … must be less than 98465. The other two ran for 25 minutes without a problem. So this is a risk with a probability, not a wall. Whether a run hits a bad frame in the first five minutes or the fifth hour depends on the shuffle order. Our Lance run read 2.56M shuffled samples without hitting it, because Lance looks up frames by integer index in the byte index instead of converting a timestamp into a position.

If a dataset is small enough to fit in the page cache, read it from local disk. On a 20,000-frame ALOHA dataset, upstream reading locally beat Lance reading from S3 (538 vs 452 samples/s). Lance’s advantage is random access at a scale where caching stops working.

02The training table is also the index

This is the part that compounds. Parquet is a columnar file format. It has statistics and row groups, but it has no secondary indexes. No vector index, no full-text index, nothing to look things up by. So as soon as you want to find frames instead of scanning them, you need a second system:

parquet + mp4

→embeddings go into a vector database
→text goes into a search service
→scores go into a metrics table
→a manifest file joins all of it back to frames
→and the trainer reads none of these. It reads the files, so any of them can drift from what you actually trained on

four systems, one source of truth, none of them overlapping

one Lance table

→a vector index on an embedding column
→a full-text index on the instruction column
→derived scores are ordinary columns
→the join is the row itself
→and it is the same table the DataLoader reads, at a pinned version

29.7 s vector index · 7.0 s FTS index · 10–54 ms queries

Here is what that table looks like. It is an ordinary Lance table, with one row per frame and the camera streams in a second table as mp4 blobs. Everything in this section is a column or an index on it.

Adding a feature column is one declaration

Every curation method needs the same thing: a score computed from the trajectory, stored next to it, and recomputed when the model changes. Whether you then drop the row or emit a label like "Advantage: positive" is a one-line difference downstream of the same column. So the column is the real artifact. Here, it is a declaration rather than a pipeline:

declare the column, then fill it in

@udf(data_type=pa.float32(), input_columns=["action_joint_velocity"],
     max_checkpoint_size=8192)
def jerk_score(v):                      # per-frame motion roughness
    ...

tbl.add_columns({"jerk_score": jerk_score})   # 0.016 s -- nothing computed yet
tbl.backfill("jerk_score", concurrency=8)     # 610,403 rows in 16.7 s

36,551 rows/s · the table grew 7% · none of the 9.9 GB of video was rewritten · readers on the old version keep working

For a feature that needs pixels, the same decorator takes num_gpus=1 and reads the blob column directly. take_blobs() returns a file-like object, and the decoder reads byte ranges out of it. There is no local copy and no dataset class:

the GPU version, reading pixels from the blob column

@udf(data_type=pa.list_(pa.float32(), 768), num_gpus=1,
     input_columns=["episode_index", "frame_index"], max_checkpoint_size=1024)
class EmbedFromBlob:                    # stateful: SigLIP2 loads once per worker
    def __call__(self, episode_index, frame_index):
        blob  = self.videos.take_blobs("video_bytes", indices=[vrow])[0]
        frame = VideoDecoder(blob).get_frames_at([pos]).data[0]

610,403 frames · 712 frames/s on 2 GPUs · 0% zero vectors

concurrency was the only scaling knob we touched. Checkpointing is real, and the stage breakdown attributes 7% of the runtime to it. But we killed a job twice and both restarts recomputed from scratch, so treat crash-resume as documented rather than measured here.

Then the columns work together

Three columns of different origin now sit on this table: an embedding from a vision model over the video blob, a score from a UDF over joint velocities, and the success flag that shipped with the dataset. A question that spans all three is one query, not a four-way join:

semantic search with a filter on a derived column

T.search(vec("a gripper closing on an object"),
         vector_column_name="emb_siglip2") \
 .where("jerk_score > 1.2875")          # the roughest 1% of frames
 .limit(4)
“a gripper closing on an object” 32.0 ms

WHERE jerk_score > 1.2875. It looks like a grasp, and the motion is in the roughest 1%.

“a cluttered kitchen counter” 27.4 ms

WHERE is_episode_successful = false. It looks like clutter, and the episode failed.

Retrieved frames with their jerk_score. The filters hold. The first set is above the 99th-percentile roughness threshold and the second is below the 95th. Text-to-frame retrieval over robot video is not a solved problem, though. The best purpose-built encoder reports 7% recall@1 on AgiBot. This narrows down a slice of data before an expensive step. It is not a search box.

What one scan over the same table found

A full curation pass over all 27,630,375 rows reads 2.52 GB in 190 seconds and decodes no video. Three findings were worth the trip:

  • openpi’s own idle filter drops 11.66% of DROID. We reimplemented it from their source. Their code never actually computes it: def __len__: return 20_000_000 # easier than iterating.
  • The default split leaks everything. A naive 80/20 split puts 100% of the validation buildings and 100% of the collectors into training too. That is all 72 buildings and all 78 collectors.
  • The standard smoothness quality gate points the wrong way. Across 95,603 episodes, checked in 62.6 seconds, successful DROID episodes are measurably jerkier than failed ones (AUROC 0.402). A smoothness filter would preferentially delete successful data.

One more thing, quietly: task_category is byte-identical to building in 100% of rows, and date is identical to collector_id. DROID ships two duplicated columns, and the task category and collection date are lost.

Mining: finding behaviour that has no label

Curation asks which data to keep. Mining asks the opposite question: where else does this happen? That is the question that needs an index. Take one frame as the query, search the embedding column, and constrain it with SQL on the same row:

tbl.search(seed_frame_embedding, vector_column_name="emb_siglip2") \
   .where("episode_index != 2 AND is_episode_successful AND jerk_score > 1.0") \
   .limit(600)                       # then keep the nearest frame per episode

Every hit is soft fabric being dragged across furniture: a duvet, three pillows, a towel and bedding, in five different rooms. None of them share the query’s task string. 0 of 8 are exact text matches, while 5 of 8 are the same physical behaviour. There is no fabric_manipulation column to filter on, and a text search for duvet would have missed every one of them, because the operators wrote “pillow”, “towel” and “bedding”.

That is the case for keeping the index next to the frames. The query mixes a vector search, two boolean columns and a derived score. It returns in 55 to 81 ms, and it hands back rows the DataLoader can train on directly. Same table, same version, and no manifest joining a vector database to object storage.

What this curation is worth, measured closed-loop

Search and mining are only useful if the training set they produce makes a better robot. DROID has no simulator, so we measured that on LIBERO, a simulation benchmark where a policy can be scored by whether it completes the task. LIBERO is also very clean: 1,693 demonstrations of 40 tasks, every one a success with the right instruction attached. Real collections are not like that, so we broke it in three ways that turn up in real teleop data, each on a random 10% of the episodes:

  • Wrong instruction. The task label is swapped for another task from the same suite.
  • Jittery actions. Noise on the arm commands, a spike on 4% of frames, the gripper flipping on 2%.
  • Out of sync. The action stream runs 0.6 seconds ahead of the observations, like a timestamp bug.

The pixels never change. All three defects live in the tabular part of the data, which is where real logging bugs live too. Then we trained SmolVLA the same way four times, 40,000 steps each, and scored each model in the simulator on 10 rollouts of every task, 400 per model.

trained onepisodesspatialobject goallibero_10all 40 tasks
the clean dataset1,6939187887886.0
the messy dataset, 30% bad1,6937471485862.7
messy, minus what three queries flagged1,1997975856977.0
messy, minus exactly the bad episodes (oracle)1,1868486807180.2

Success rate in %, 100 rollouts per suite. Same seed, same recipe, same steps for every row. The oracle row uses the hidden list of broken episodes, which no real dataset comes with.

The mess cost 23 points. Three queries on the table got 14 back, and on the goal suite, where several tasks share one scene and differ only in the instruction, almost all of it: 48 to 85. The oracle shows what perfect cleaning would have bought: 80.2, so roughly 3 of the remaining 9 points come from the 33 bad episodes that slipped through and roughly 6 from training on 30% fewer episodes.

The three queries are the same mechanism as the columns above: one column and one rule per defect, thresholds set as robust z-scores within each task, and nothing that knows which episodes were broken.

  • Jitter gets a per-frame jerk_score, how much the arm command changes between frames. Episodes far above their task's median are flagged.
  • Out of sync gets a per-episode act_lag: how many frames you have to shift the commanded motion before it best explains the motion the robot actually made. Clean logs peak at zero.
  • Wrong instruction gets a per-episode goal_dist: how far the last frame's embedding sits from the median last frame of every other episode with the same label.

three columns, one filter

frames.merge(per_frame,   left_on="index",         right_on="index")          # jerk_score
frames.merge(per_episode, left_on="episode_index", right_on="episode_index")  # act_lag, goal_dist, quality_flag

keep = frames.to_table(columns=["episode_index"],
                       filter="quality_flag = 'ok'")   # 1,199 episodes -> --dataset.episodes

0.2 s to write the columns · table version 1 → 6 · no video touched · the trainer reads the episode list, nothing is copied

The weak spot is worth knowing. Almost every wrong label that slipped through is in the spatial suite, where all ten tasks end with the same bowl on the same plate, so the last frame cannot tell the labels apart and neither can a check built on it.

The mess here was injected. The three defect types are real ones, taken from what turns up in teleop collections, and the queries make no use of knowing they were there. The rates, 10% each, are ours. On your data the mix will differ, and so will which check does the work. The scripts that broke LIBERO and the ones that found the damage are in the companion repo.

And you can watch it without converting it

The same byte-range reads the trainer uses also drive a viewer. You can scrub through any episode of the 369 GB dataset straight from object storage. There is no download and no MCAP conversion step, because the mp4 bytes are already a column in the table.

lerobot-dataset-viz --repo-id ... --root s3://bucket/data.lance --display-mode foxglove

03What the models did

We trained for 10,000 steps from S3. To measure what that bought, we compared two checkpoints from the same run, one at 80 steps and one at 10,000, on 100 held-out episodes the model never trained on. Both checkpoints share identical action-normalization statistics, which is what makes the two numbers comparable.

Held-out loss falls from 0.4777 to 0.2165, which is 54.7% lower. Action-chunk MAE falls from 0.5130 to 0.3706, and next-action MAE from 0.3259 to 0.1004. 48 of 48 held-out episodes improved.

The improvement holds across the range of how much the arm actually moves. By motion quartile it is 70.5%, 71.2%, 71.4% and 64.0%, so it is not an artifact of easy, near-static episodes. If anything, the correlation runs the other way: busier episodes improve slightly less (r = −0.45).

DROID has no simulator, so closed-loop success rates are not available. What we can measure is whether the policy predicts the actions the teleoperator actually took on an episode it never saw. That is what the recording at the top of this post shows, on episode 226.

Then we asked whether curation helps on data that is already clean. We trained three models for 1,500 steps each and tested them on the same 100 held-out episodes. Training on all 646 episodes gave a held-out loss of 0.3686. A diversity-selected half gave 0.5082, and a random half gave 0.5238. We also ran the mining loop above end to end: score every frame with the trained model's own error, mine the episodes most like its worst frames, and fine-tune on those against a random set of the same size. The mined set matched random within 0.002 on held-out action error, and fine-tuning on the highest-error episodes outright hurt, by 0.025, because the model's error tracks how fast the arm moves rather than how good the demonstration is.

On clean data, which episodes you keep barely matters, and the obvious heuristics can make things worse. That matches the literature. One study measured naive velocity filtering as worse than no curation at all, and a recent audit found that the quality metric best at detecting bad data produced the worst policy. On messy data the same kind of queries were worth 14 points of success in section 02.

That is the point. The value of a data layer is not that it subsets your data cleverly. It is that the score column, the embedding column, the index and the split all live on the rows the trainer reads, at a version you can reopen. So when you check a widely recommended heuristic and find it points the wrong way, or find that 30% of a collection is broken, that costs you an afternoon instead of a quarter.

Try it yourself

LeRobot reads Lance datasets natively through the standard LeRobotDataset class. Install the reader and the converter, convert any LeRobot v3.0 dataset, and point your existing training code at the result. Nothing about your recording or training code changes.

pip install "lerobot[lancedb]"           # the reader, inside lerobot itself
pip install "lerobot[lancedb-convert]"   # the converter

lerobot-lance-convert --repo-id lerobot/pusht --out ./pusht-lance

The full walkthrough, including loading from S3, training from the CLI and viewing episodes in Foxglove, is in the LeRobot integration docs. Ready-made Lance datasets to try are under the lance-format organisation on Hugging Face.

Reproduction scripts, the full measurement log including withdrawn numbers, and the upstream issues we filed along the way are in the companion repo. Disclosure: LanceDB publishes this benchmark and maintains the LeRobot integration. The upstream code measured here is unmodified except where a fix is named.
